caption:
A single radar return is a number, not a verdict. Backscatter changes with soil moisture, vegetation structure, surface roughness, even look angle from one pass to the next. Read in isolation, it tells you almost nothing.

What makes it useful is a baseline — the same patch of ground, same time of year, compared across multiple prior passes. An anomaly is a deviation from that history, not a raw value crossing some fixed threshold. Build the baseline wrong and every flood plain looks like a flood, every dry season looks like drought.

This is why a monitoring system is only as good as its archive. A new area of interest starts with reduced confidence until enough history accumulates to know what normal looks like there.
thread: A radar pixel by itself tells you almost nothing. Backscatter shifts with soil moisture, vegetation, surface roughness, even the angle of the pass. Raw value, no context, is not a detection.
What turns it into a signal is a baseline — the same ground, same season, compared against a run of prior passes. An anomaly is a deviation from that history, not a number crossing a fixed line.
Get the baseline wrong and a normal flood plain reads as a flood every wet season. A new area of interest starts on reduced confidence until enough passes accumulate to know what normal looks like.
This is unglamorous work — archive-building, not detection. But it's the part that decides whether an alert means anything.

card.headline: A pixel means nothing without a baseline
card.sub: Radar backscatter shifts with moisture, vegetation, and angle. An anomaly is a deviation from history — not a raw number crossing a line.

rationale: Introduces a genuinely new mechanic (baseline construction for change detection) not covered in prior posts, keeps strict BLUF/analyst voice, and avoids any pitch or hard-rule violation.
